findings.surface: EC2 Auto Scaling: scheduled actions / clock
findings.claim: PutScheduledUpdateGroupAction and BatchPutScheduledUpdateGroupAction store actions and even resolve a next occurrence instant, but at HEAD no code path ever evaluates a stored action against wall-clock time: neither a one-time StartTime nor a Recurrence changes a group's MinSize/MaxSize/DesiredCapacity, launches/terminates instances, or records a scaling activity. AWS applies the action at the occurrence and records an activity for it.
findings.root_cause: The EC2 Auto Scaling clock is a request-driven due-instant sweep (materialize_due) plus a lifecycle-event pump. Both enumerate only pending cooldown-gated capacity changes, transient instance states, health-check debts, warm pools, instance refreshes, lifecycle-hook timeouts and queued events. group.scheduled_actions is never part of next_clock_due_at and materialize_due never reads it, so the only ASG scheduled-action code is PUT/DESCRIBE storage and a cron parser used once at write time. The sibling Application Auto Scaling crate has the missing executor, so this is a per-service clock gap, not a missing library capability.

findings.surface: EC2 Auto Scaling: scheduled-action validation, retention, batch semantics
findings.claim: At HEAD four of the five causes in the scheduled-actions doc persist: a one-time action whose EndTime passed is still listed; StartTime/EndTime sub-second fractions are echoed verbatim; a StartTime in the past is accepted (no 'Given start time is in the past' refusal anywhere in the repo); malformed Recurrence is checked only AFTER the capacity-bound check and hence reports the wrong reason. findings.root_cause: ScheduledActionPut::validate has no absolute-time check, no recurrence-first ordering and no truncation; StoredScheduledAction::from_put/view carry DateTime verbatim; DescribeScheduledActions filters only on the requested start-time window and nothing retires spent actions; BatchPut loops put_scheduled_action (an upsert) per entry and collects failures only from validation refusals, with no atomic rollback.

findings.surface: cross-service architecture: clocks, timers, due instants
findings.claim: The clustered gaps share one structural cause: there is no shared clock/scheduler in core/ or vendor/. Instead 22 hand-rolled drive_*clock tasks live in 21 service crates, each started by a request handler, each with its own bounded wake-up cap (17 crates have explicit MAX_CLOCK_TICKS/MAX_CLOCK_WAKE_UPS constants), and each service decides independently which due instants to register. Auto Scaling's scheduled actions, EC2's instance state-change events and ECS's blue/green bake/stages are absent from their services' clocks, while EventBridge rules, EventBridge Scheduler and Application Auto Scaling scheduled actions do have working clocks. Wall-clock durations are also compressed to fixed short spans (500ms/2s/3s/5s) regardless of the caller's minutes/seconds values.
findings.root_cause: Per-service, request-started, in-process tokio pumps with finite tick budgets plus request-driven materialize_due sweeps. A time-driven behavior only exists if its own service registers a due instant and starts a pump; a new feature (scheduled actions, event emission, blue/green stages) that forgets either step silently never runs. The pumps are not durable across a restart and stop after their cap unless another request restarts them.
